### 7. The client spoke a protocol neither OTP flow reads — reconciled on the client side

`ITEM-44` · readiness · `PARALLEL-EXECUTION-NEUTRAL`

core/data-client.js sends action "otpGenerate"/"otpVerify" from config/endpoints.config.js and nests everything under payload; both OTP flows switch on action "generate"/"verify" and read identifier and otp_code at the top level. Neither the dispatch value nor the field placement matches, so the Switch matches no case and neither OTP path runs. This is not caused by the ITEM-43 cutover — the old flow has the same case values — and is consistent with ITEM-2: nothing has ever exercised it. It fails loudly: varStatusCode starts at 500 and the Response returns it, so an unmatched request answers 500 rather than a misleading 200. Two further findings sit alongside it: Case_Generate mails the code to the literal dgsregistry@nitda.gov.ng rather than to the requester, and writes item/Title from identifier with no coalesce while the verify lookup binds on Title through a four-way one — so a caller sending userEmail writes an empty Title that verify can never match.

**Where it stands.** APPLIED_UNVERIFIED · none established; no item in this register carries a target date

**Do**

1. Done — the client sends action generate/verify with identifier and otp_code at the top level.
2. Done — npm run test:otpprotocol asserts the seam against the deployed definitions.
3. Outstanding — the recipient decision: Case_Generate mails the code to the literal dgsregistry@nitda.gov.ng rather than to the requester. That is a flow change and an agency call.
4. Outstanding — run the four cutover tests through the platform (ITEM-43).

**Bring**

- DIRECTION SETTLED 2026-09-04: reconcile on the CLIENT, not the flows. The two flows already agree with each other — Web - OTP Generate and IP_OTP_VERIFY both read identifier and otp_code at the top level and switch on generate/verify — so the client was the single outlier and one change fixes both. Changing the flows instead would mean a second designer paste into a flow certified hours earlier, plus a change to a second flow nobody has reviewed, to reach the same place.
- The mechanism is the client's own: flatPayload already existed for flows that read their fields where they were sent, and modules/single-assignment.js already uses it. No new mechanism was introduced.
- Blast radius is nil: each endpoint's action is an independent frozen entry and flatPayload is per-call, so no other endpoint's wire format changed. The options passthrough added to invokeObsidianAction is additive — every existing caller passes two arguments and gets {}.
- The estate has two conventions and both are correct: the portal posts flat bodies with no action because one flow serves one endpoint; the internal runtime dispatches {action, payload} because DYNAMIC_ACTIONS and EMAIL share a flow. The OTP flows are switch-dispatched, so they need an action — the disagreement was vocabulary, not architecture.

**Done when.** One request from the platform reaches a matched Switch case, and one code issued through the platform verifies through the platform. Until both are observed against the tenant, this is unresolved regardless of what the code reads like.

### 16. None of the four HTTP governance endpoints returns an outcome to its caller

`GOV-04` · governance · `PARALLEL-EXECUTION-NEUTRAL`

In all four cases the caller receives Power Automate's default acknowledgement and never learns what happened. Reachability, status/runStatus agreement and body determinism are asserted by tests/governance-flow-corrections.test.mjs. · tenant: OUTSTANDING. The deployed flows are unchanged until GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md Step 4 is applied.

**Do**

- Give each of the four a Response action on every path — success and each Terminate branch — carrying the estate's response envelope, and place it before the Terminate rather than after the scope. For 05, move `Reply` inside the scope ahead of the terminations, or drop it: unreachable code that looks like a reply is worse than none.

**Done when.** Give each of the four a Response action on every path — success and each Terminate branch — carrying the estate's response envelope, and place it before the Terminate rather than after the scope. ### 17. The retirement endpoint cascades unconditionally, and anyone holding its URL can call it

`GOV-05` · governance · `SEQUENCE-DEPENDENT`

05 - GOV - Retire HTTP Flow accepts an anonymous POST of {environmentId, flowId, retirementReason} — triggerAuthenticationType All, so the SAS signature in the URL is the whole of the authentication. It then retires the registry row, closes every current contract version, and marks every non-retired consumer and every non-retired dependency as Retired, before resolving the flow's open exceptions. The workbook's own key control for this scenario reads: 'verify no active consumers/dependencies remain' and 'stop new traffic before technical removal'. The flow does not verify. It retires them, which erases the evidence that any were active.

**Where it stands.** repository: CORRECTED DEFINITION PRODUCED. The cascade is gated by If_Safe_To_Retire: both active counts are taken before any write, retirement is blocked with 409 when either is non-zero, and proceeds only when both are zero or force is true. Retire_Registry was lifted out of If_Registry_Found, where it would otherwise have escaped the guard — a defect the test found, not the design. A forced retirement is recorded with both counts. · tenant: OUTSTANDING. GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md Step 4.3 validates all four paths against the live flow.

**Do**

- Implement the documented control: count active consumers and dependencies first and refuse the retirement when any exist, returning them to the caller so the owner can act. Keep the cascade behind an explicit force flag that is recorded on the registry row. Consider whether an operation this destructive should be anonymous at all — Tenant authentication is available and is what IP_SCAN_INTAKE already uses.

**Done when.** Implement the documented control: count active consumers and dependencies first and refuse the retirement when any exist, returning them to the caller so the owner can act. ## The flow registry, end to end

109 rows, 168 flow-to-list edges, 7 lists that do
not exist yet. Nothing here needs analysis; it needs a tenant session and four columns.

| | Do | Who | Where |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Run the provisioner in a browser on DGO_ECM_GOVERNANCE. | tenant administrator | npm run governance:registryprovisioner emits it; it is dry-run by default. |
| 2 | Record the seven GUIDs it returns. | tenant administrator | docs/reference/governance-list-registry.json |
| 3 | Ratify or override the proposed SystemName and Criticality. | the agency | docs/reference/REGISTRY_DECISIONS.md |
| 4 | Supply a technical owner for every flow. | the agency | The one column nothing can propose. |
| 5 | Seed the rows. | operator | docs/reference/FLOW_REGISTRY_SEED.json |

**The four columns are the whole blocker.** 83 of the blanks are proposals to
ratify or override; 244 must be authored, of which every row needs a technical
owner. See [`REGISTRY_DECISIONS.md`](../reference/REGISTRY_DECISIONS.md).

## The one ordering that is irreversible

**GOV-09** — It does not block the endpoint commissioning path, which touches no governance list. It blocks the DELETE phase of Step 3, and it re-orders the runbook: Step 4 before Step 3.4.

---

## How to check any of this

```bash
npm run master        # every open item, with what would close it
npm run outstanding   # the total, across all five registers
npm run external      # regenerate this document
npm run commission    # what a commissioning run reports today
```

Every step above is an open item in a register. When the register says it has closed, the step
leaves this document on the next build. **Where this document and a command disagree, the command
governs.**
